newsitem.title: UK: Grandmet/Guinness deal signals drinks "big bang".
newsitem.headline: Grandmet/Guinness deal signals drinks "big bang".

text.p: The 20 billion-pound ($32.5 billion) merger between Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc has signalled a "big bang" in the consumer industry which is bound to unnerve rivals like Allied Domecq and Seagram, analysts said.
"This is a big bang for the spirits industry after the last consolidation ten years ago," said Ron Littleboy, analyst at Nomura.

"It's great news for both companies, all the others will be worried sick, but what are they to do -- this group is now just so powerful and there is unlikely to be a deal open to others which offers the same scale of benefits."
Ten years ago Guinness bought United Distillers, GrandMet acquired Heublein and Allied Lyons bought Hiram Walker.

Analysts said the Guinness merger with GrandMet greatly weakened the position of drinks and retail group Allied Domecq Plc ALLD L, due to report its half year results on Tuesday. "It presents a tremendously difficult problem for Allied," said Philip Hawkins, analyst at Merrill Lynch. "They will have to look for strategic partners otherwise they will continue to see their market share erode further and continue to underperform," he said.
The most Allied can hope for is to sew up a deal with Seagram Co Ltd VO.TO or fall subject to a predator, possibly the likes of American Brands Inc AMB.N or Brown-Forman Corp BFa.N, analysts said.

"Allied and Seagram and Pernod will all be very worried. It could be the last nail in the coffin for Allied, they will have to do something dramatic now," said Littleboy. Analysts emerged shell-shocked from their meeting with the company's managment by the timing of the announcement, although a year ago an embarrassing press leak showed Guinness was looking at a bid for the company.
Analysts had generally only positive views on the deal saying the two company's complemented each other in terms of brands and geographic spread.

But there was concern about the role of French luxury goods company LVMH's role in the newly merged company. Bernard Arnault, chairman of LVMH which owns 14.2 percent of Guinness, voted against the merger at a meeting of the Guinness board on May 9.

Nick Lyall, an analyst at SocGen said "there is a bit of a question mark over what is going to happen to Arnault's stake in Guinness, and he may represent an interference as we go forward. That would be are only caveat about the deal." ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
